noteBlocks.text: 1. Rate: a change divided by a time

noteBlocks.md: A **rate of reaction** is how fast a reactant is used up or a product is made. Measure a **change**, such as the volume of gas made or the mass lost, and the **time** it took, then divide: **rate = change ÷ time**. The unit follows from the division: cm³/s for a gas volume, g/s for a mass.

noteBlocks.title: An amount is not a rate
noteBlocks.md: **27 cm³ of gas** is an amount: it says how much, not how fast. **27 cm³ in 9 s** is a rate once you divide: 3 cm³ every second, or 3 cm³/s. Two reactions can make the same amount of gas at very different rates.

noteBlocks.stem: Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. After 20 s the gas syringe holds 38 cm³ of hydrogen. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 20 s. [2]

steps.working: change = 38 cm³ of hydrogen; time = 20 s
steps.decision: A rate needs two measurements: how much changed and how long it took. The syringe started empty, so the whole reading is the change.

steps.working: rate = change ÷ time = 38 ÷ 20
steps.decision: Change on top, time underneath. The other way up gives seconds per cm³, which is not a rate.

steps.working: rate = 1.9 cm³/s
steps.decision: The unit is the change's unit over seconds: cm³ divided by s.

noteBlocks.prompt: Zinc reacts with dilute acid. After 26 s the gas syringe holds 39 cm³ of hydrogen. What is the mean rate, in cm³/s?
noteBlocks.explain: 39 ÷ 26 = 1.5 cm³/s: the change over the time, as step 2 of See it divided, with the unit from step 3.

twin.prompt: A flask on a balance loses 0.84 g in the first 42 s. What is the mean rate of mass loss, in g/s?
twin.explain: 0.84 ÷ 42 = 0.02 g/s: the same division as step 2 of See it, with grams over seconds.

noteBlocks.text: 2. Three ways to follow a reaction

noteBlocks.md: CCEA allows three measurements. **Collect the gas** in a gas syringe and read its volume at fixed times: magnesium or marble chips with acid, or hydrogen peroxide breaking down over a manganese(IV) oxide catalyst. **Weigh the flask** on a top-pan balance and record its mass as the gas escapes. **Time a precipitate**: sodium thiosulfate and acid turn cloudy and hide a cross under the flask.

noteBlocks.title: Why the balance suits carbon dioxide
noteBlocks.md: The balance only sees the mass of the gas that leaves. Carbon dioxide is heavy enough to show up. Hydrogen is so light that magnesium and acid barely move the reading, so follow hydrogen with a gas syringe instead.

noteBlocks.stem: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen when manganese(IV) oxide is added. Suggest a method to follow the rate of this reaction. [3]

steps.working: Put the hydrogen peroxide in a conical flask, add the manganese(IV) oxide and fit the bung and delivery tube to a gas syringe straight away.
steps.decision: A gas is given off, so collect it. The bung goes in at once so no oxygen escapes.

steps.working: Start the stopclock as the catalyst goes in.
steps.decision: Timing starts the moment the reactants meet.

steps.working: Read the volume of oxygen in the syringe at fixed times, such as every 10 s, until it stops changing.
steps.decision: Say what you measure, with what, and when: a volume, in the syringe, at known times.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student times how long a cross under a flask takes to disappear. Which reaction is she following?
options: sodium thiosulfate with acid
marble chips with acid
magnesium with acid
noteBlocks.explain: Only sodium thiosulfate and acid make a precipitate, the cloudiness that hides the cross. The reactions that give off a gas are followed with a syringe or a balance, as step 1 of See it chose for the oxygen.

optionNotes.why: Marble chips and acid give carbon dioxide: the mixture fizzes but stays clear, so nothing ever hides the cross.
Magnesium and acid give hydrogen and a clear solution; no precipitate forms to hide the cross.

twin.prompt: A flask stands on a top-pan balance with cotton wool in its neck. What does the student record?
options: the mass at fixed times
the volume of gas at fixed times
the time for a cross to disappear
twin.explain: A balance reads mass: as the gas escapes through the cotton wool the reading falls, and it is read at fixed times, just as step 3 of See it read the syringe.

optionNotes.option: the volume of gas at fixed times
optionNotes.why: A balance reads mass, not volume; here the gas leaves through the cotton wool and is never collected.

optionNotes.option: the time for a cross to disappear
optionNotes.why: That is the precipitate method. A balance follows the mass the flask loses as its gas escapes.

noteBlocks.md: Sometimes you time one fixed change: a cross disappearing, a strip of magnesium vanishing, or a set volume of gas collecting. There is no amount to divide, so use **rate = 1 ÷ time**, with the time in seconds and the unit **s⁻¹**. A shorter time gives a bigger rate, which is why the time goes underneath.

noteBlocks.title: Three decimal places means three
noteBlocks.md: When a question says 'give your answer to 3 decimal places', the answer mark needs exactly three: 0.040, not 0.04. In 2025 this instruction cost candidates the mark at both tiers.

noteBlocks.stem: Sodium thiosulfate and acid are mixed in a flask over a cross. The cross disappears after 25 s. Calculate the rate of reaction, to 3 decimal places. [2]

steps.working: rate = 1 ÷ time = 1 ÷ 25
steps.decision: One fixed change was timed, so the rule is one over the time, in seconds.
Do the division before any rounding.

steps.working: rate = 0.040 s⁻¹
steps.decision: Three decimal places means three digits after the point, so the final zero stays. One over seconds is s⁻¹.

noteBlocks.prompt: In another run the cross disappears after 17 s. What is the rate, in s⁻¹, to 3 decimal places?
noteBlocks.explain: 1 ÷ 17 = 0.0588…, which is 0.059 to 3 decimal places: one over the time, as step 1 of See it wrote it, then rounded as step 3 did.

twin.prompt: A strip of magnesium ribbon disappears in acid after 35 s. What is the rate, in s⁻¹, to 3 decimal places?
twin.explain: 1 ÷ 35 = 0.0286…, so 0.029 s⁻¹ to 3 decimal places: the same rule as step 1 of See it.

noteBlocks.md: Plot the syringe readings against time and the curve tells you three things. Its **steepness** is the rate, so the reaction is fastest at the start, when there is most of each reactant. Where it **goes flat**, the reaction has stopped because a reactant is used up. The **height** of the flat part is the total gas made.

noteBlocks.title: Where this mark goes
noteBlocks.md: The syringe is never emptied, so each reading already holds all the gas so far. In 2025's Booklet B a sizeable number added every volume in the table instead of reading the total off their graph.

steps.decision: The flat height is the total. Adding the readings would count the same gas again and again.

steps.working: (b) It first reaches 70 cm³ at 80 s, so the reaction finished at 80 s.
steps.decision: Find where the climb stops, not where the graph ends: it runs on to 120 s.

steps.working: (c) Between 0 and 20 s, where the curve is steepest.
steps.decision: Steepest means the most gas each second, while the magnesium and the acid are most plentiful.

noteBlocks.prompt: A gas syringe reads 0, 33, 51, 62, 66 and 66 cm³ at 20 s intervals. What total volume of gas was made, in cm³?
noteBlocks.explain: 66 cm³, the last reading, where the readings stop changing: each one is a running total, as step 1 of See it read the flat height. Adding them gives 278, which counts the same gas over and over.

twin.prompt: A gas syringe reads 0, 21, 34, 41, 44 and 44 cm³, one reading every 30 s from the start. At what time did the reaction finish, in s?
twin.explain: The readings first reach 44 cm³ at the fifth reading, 4 × 30 = 120 s, and stop changing there, as step 2 of See it found the finish.

noteBlocks.md: For the mean rate between two times, read the volume at **both** times, take the **change** (later minus earlier) and divide by the **time between them**, not by the later time. On the same curve a later interval gives a smaller rate: the reaction slows as the reactants are used up.

noteBlocks.title: Where this specification stops
noteBlocks.md: Other boards find the rate at one instant by drawing a tangent to the curve, and some videos show it. CCEA does not ask for tangents: a mean rate between two times is as far as it goes.

noteBlocks.why: A mean rate worked off a curve, beside our own steps; skip its tangent part.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the same magnesium curve the volume is 58 cm³ at 40 s and 70 cm³ at 80 s. What is the mean rate between 40 s and 80 s, in cm³/s?
noteBlocks.explain: (70 − 58) ÷ (80 − 40) = 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3 cm³/s: the change and the time between, as step 2 and step 3 of See it took them.

twin.prompt: A flask on a balance has lost 2.46 g after 30 s and 3.06 g after 80 s. What is the mean rate of mass loss between those times, in g/s?
twin.explain: (3.06 − 2.46) ÷ (80 − 30) = 0.60 ÷ 50 = 0.012 g/s: change over the time between, as step 4 of See it divided.

noteBlocks.md: A curve goes flat when one reactant runs out, so **the amount of that reactant decides the final height**. Heat the mixture or use a powder, with the same amounts, and the curve is steeper and flat sooner, at the **same height**. Change the amount of the reactant that runs out and the height changes: the same volume of acid at half the concentration, with the other reactant in excess, makes **half the product**.

noteBlocks.alt: Three curves of product against time: the original; a faster run, level sooner at the same height; and a run with half the acid, less steep and level at half the height.
noteBlocks.caption: Faster with the same amounts: the same height. Half the reactant that runs out: half the height.

noteBlocks.stem: Sodium thiosulfate, in excess, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and the mass of precipitate levels off at 6 g. Describe the curve you would expect (a) at a higher temperature [2] and (b) with the same volume of acid at half the concentration. [2]

steps.working: The thiosulfate is in excess, so the acid runs out first: the acid sets the final mass.
steps.decision: Find the reactant that runs out; its amount fixes the height.

steps.working: (a) Steeper from the start and flat sooner, still levelling off at 6 g.
steps.decision: The same amounts of both reactants make the same mass of precipitate, only sooner.

steps.working: (b) Half the concentration in the same volume is half the acid, so the curve levels off at 3 g.
steps.decision: In 2025 most Higher candidates lost this mark by levelling the new curve at the original height.

steps.working: (b) It also rises less steeply than the original, because the acid is less concentrated.
steps.decision: Two things describe any new curve: how steep it is and where it levels off.

noteBlocks.prompt: Marble chips, in excess, react with 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid, and 76 cm³ of carbon dioxide is made. The run is repeated with 25 cm³ of acid at half the concentration. Where does the new curve level off?
options: at 38 cm³
at 76 cm³
at 152 cm³
noteBlocks.explain: The chips are in excess, so the acid decides the height. Half the concentration in the same volume is half the acid, so half the gas: 38 cm³, as step 3 of See it halved the precipitate.

optionNotes.why: The acid runs out first here, so halving it halves the gas; the height stays only when the amounts stay.
Less acid cannot make more gas: a weaker acid is slower, and here it also gives less.

twin.prompt: The same run, with the chips in excess and 25 cm³ of the original acid, is repeated at a higher temperature. Where does the new curve level off?
options: at 76 cm³, but sooner
at 38 cm³
above 76 cm³
twin.explain: Nothing about the amounts has changed, so the same 76 cm³ is made, only sooner, as step 2 of See it kept the precipitate at its height.

optionNotes.why: Heating changes how fast, not how much: the amounts are the same, so the gas made is the same.
A faster reaction makes the same gas sooner, not more of it.

noteBlocks.md: **The mass graph runs downhill.** Weigh the flask and plot its mass: the curve falls and levels off when the gas stops. A faster run with the same amounts falls more steeply, **below** the original, to the **same** final mass. In 2024 curves drawn above the original, or two lines for one run, lost marks.

**The unit is its own mark.** When a question says 'state the units', write g/s for a mass, cm³/s for a volume and s⁻¹ for 1 ÷ time; in 2024 many lost this mark. **One rate, not four**: in 2025 some worked out every rate in the table when one was asked.

noteBlocks.prompt: The balance run is repeated with the acid cooled and the same amounts. Where does the new mass curve run?
options: above the original, ending at the same mass
below the original, ending at the same mass
above the original, ending at a higher mass
noteBlocks.answer: above the original, ending at the same mass
noteBlocks.explain: Cooler means slower, so the mass is lost later and the curve stays above the original. The same amounts still lose the same gas, so it ends at the same mass: the reverse of step 4 of See it.

optionNotes.option: below the original, ending at the same mass
optionNotes.why: Below is a faster run, losing mass sooner. Cooler acid is slower, so the mass falls later and the curve stays above.

optionNotes.option: above the original, ending at a higher mass
optionNotes.why: The same amounts lose the same mass of gas in the end, so the final mass is the same.

twin.prompt: The balance run is repeated with the acid warmed and the same amounts. Where does the new mass curve run?
options: below the original, ending at the same mass
above the original, ending at the same mass
below the original, ending at a lower mass
twin.answer: below the original, ending at the same mass
twin.explain: Warmer is faster, so the mass falls sooner and the curve runs below; the same amounts end at the same mass, as step 4 of See it drew for the powder.

optionNotes.option: above the original, ending at the same mass
optionNotes.why: Above is a slower run. Warmer acid is faster, so the mass falls sooner and the curve drops below.

optionNotes.option: below the original, ending at a lower mass
optionNotes.why: Faster does not lose more gas: the same amounts end at the same final mass.

noteBlocks.prompt: A rate worked out as 1 ÷ time, with the time in seconds, has the unit ______.
noteBlocks.answer: s⁻¹ | s-1 | s^-1 | /s | per second | per s
noteBlocks.explain: Grams over seconds gave g/s in step 3 of See it; one over seconds gives s⁻¹, read as 'per second'.

twin.prompt: A rate worked out from a volume in cm³ over a time in seconds has the unit ______.
twin.answer: cm³/s | cm3/s | cm^3/s | cm³ s⁻¹ | cm3 s-1 | cm^3 s^-1 | cm³ per second | cm3 per second | cubic centimetres per second
twin.explain: A volume over a time: cm³ over s, written cm³/s, just as step 3 of See it wrote grams over seconds as g/s.

noteBlocks.md:
Work out a rate as change ÷ time, in cm³/s or g/s, or as 1 ÷ time, in s⁻¹.
Choose a method: a gas syringe, a balance, or a cross hidden by a precipitate.
Read the total off the flat part and the finish from where it goes flat.
Find a mean rate between two times from the change and the time between.
Sketch a changed run: the reactant that runs out sets the height.

Measuring rates is set most years: Q7 of both C2 papers in 2024 and 2025, early in the 2021 and 2026 Higher papers, and in Booklet B. Expect a graph to plot or read, a rate to stated places with its unit, and a sketch of a changed run. Stuck? Write rate = change ÷ time, then name the change and the time.

steps.working: Follow the curve to the right until it stops rising. It runs flat at 54 cm³, so the total volume of gas is 54 cm³.
steps.decision: Read the total off the flat part of the curve. Adding the volumes in the table counts the same gas over and over, and Summer 2025's report names it as a real error.

options: Because the syringe reading is a running total already, so the last one is the whole lot
Because each reading is the gas made since the last reading
Because the table stops before the reaction does
whyMenu.explain: The syringe never empties, so every reading includes all the gas made so far. The final reading is the total.

accepted: Follow the curve to the right until it stops rising. It runs flat at 54 cm³, so the total volume of gas is 54 cm³.

steps.working: The curve becomes flat at 50 s, so the reaction finished at 50 s.
steps.decision: Flat means nothing more is happening. The table runs on to 60 s, but the reaction was over before that.

accepted: The curve becomes flat at 50 s, so the reaction finished at 50 s.

steps.working: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken
steps.decision: Write the rule before the numbers. The rule is what tells you which number goes on top.

accepted: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken

any: change in volume divided by time

steps.working: rate = 54 ÷ 50
steps.decision: Substitute the time the reaction took, 50 s, not the last time in the table. Dividing by 60 s gives 0.9 cm³/s and loses the answer mark.

accepted: rate = 54 ÷ 50

steps.working: rate = 1.08 cm³/s
steps.decision: Two decimal places because the question said so, and the unit is the volume unit over seconds.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 54 cm³. (b) 50 s. (c) rate = change ÷ time = 54 ÷ 50 = 1.08 cm³/s.

twin.stem: A different run, with more marble chips and a more concentrated acid, is followed on a balance. After 200 s the flask has lost 3.60 g and the reading has stopped falling. Calculate the mean rate of reaction in g/s, to three decimal places.

items.stem: Which of these is a unit of volume?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 — reading units; you are not expected to have met rates yet

options.feedback: Cubic centimetres. Every gas-syringe reading in this lesson is in cm³.
Grams measure mass. Both turn up in this topic, so it is worth separating them before you start.
Seconds measure time. The rate unit puts a volume over a time, so you need to be able to tell them apart.

items.stem: A car travels 90 km in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
items.skill: Prerequisite from mathematics — a rate is an amount divided by a time

options.feedback: 90 ÷ 3 = 30. Every rate in chemistry is built the same way: the change divided by the time.
That multiplies. A rate divides the amount by the time, so 90 ÷ 3 = 30 km/h.
That is the time divided by the distance, which is the fraction upside down. Section 1 of the lesson is about which number goes on top.

items.stem: Marble chips are calcium carbonate. Which gas is given off when they react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.8 — reactions of acids with carbonates

options.feedback: Acid plus a carbonate always gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide. That gas is what every method in this lesson is following.
Hydrogen comes from an acid with a metal. With a carbonate the gas is carbon dioxide, and limewater turning milky is the test.
Oxygen comes from hydrogen peroxide with a catalyst, which is one of the other reactions on this specification. A carbonate gives carbon dioxide.

items.stem: A gas syringe reads 0, 22, 36, 46, 52, 54 and 54 cm³ at 10 s intervals. What total volume of gas was produced?
items.skill: Read a total from a set of syringe readings

options.feedback: The readings are a running total, so the last one is the whole amount. On a graph it is the height of the flat stretch.
That adds every reading together, counting the same gas six times over. Summer 2025's Booklet B report names this exact error.
That is the gas made after the first 20 s only. The total is everything collected from the start.
That is the reading after 10 s, not the total. Follow the readings to the end, where they stop changing.

items.stem: A reaction produces 54 cm³ of gas and the curve goes flat at 50 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.feedback: 54 ÷ 50 = 1.08. Volume on top, time underneath, unit cm³/s.
That is the time divided by the volume, the fraction upside down. Rate is always the change on top.
That divides by the last time printed in the table. The reaction was over before then, so use the time it actually took.
That multiplies instead of dividing. A rate is an amount per second, so the time goes underneath.

items.stem: Which apparatus would you use to measure the volume of carbon dioxide given off in a reaction?
items.skill: Name the apparatus for a method

options.feedback: A gas syringe, or an inverted measuring cylinder over water. Keep the word gas: 'syringe' alone lost marks in Summer 2025.
The balance follows the mass lost, which is the other method. It never tells you a volume.
A thermometer is for the temperature-change experiments in the energy topic, not for measuring a gas.
The reaction happens in the conical flask, but the flask does not measure anything. The gas syringe does.

items.stem: In the disappearing-cross experiment the cross was hidden after 32 s. Using rate = 1 ÷ time, what is the rate?

options.feedback: 1 ÷ 32 = 0.031 s⁻¹. A longer time gives a smaller rate, which is what you want it to do.
That is the time itself, not one divided by it. The rule turns the time upside down on purpose.
That turns the time into minutes first, so the answer is per minute. The unit asked for is s⁻¹, so keep the time in seconds.
The number is right but the unit is not. One divided by a time in seconds gives a rate per second, written s⁻¹, and CCEA marks that unit separately.

items.stem: Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid and 54 cm³ of gas is made. The run is repeated with the same mass of chips crushed to a powder, and the same acid. What does the new curve do?
items.skill: Sketch the effect of a change on a rate curve

options.text: it is steeper and levels off at 54 cm³
options.feedback: Steeper because it is faster, and the same height because the same amounts of chips and acid can only make the same amount of gas.

options.text: it is steeper and levels off above 54 cm³
options.feedback: A faster reaction makes the same gas sooner, not more of it: the amounts are unchanged, so the height is too. In 2024 curves finishing at a different point lost the mark.

options.text: it is less steep and levels off at 54 cm³
options.feedback: Powder has a much larger surface area, so the reaction is faster and the curve is steeper, not shallower.

options.text: it is steeper and never levels off
options.feedback: Every curve levels off once a reactant runs out, and with the same amounts that happens at the same height as before.

items.stem: A results table has the headings 'Time' and 'Volume of gas'. What is missing?

options.feedback: Units belong in the heading, and the axis labels are copied straight from there. The missing x-axis label was the commonest lost mark in Summer 2025's Booklet B.
The rate is worked out afterwards from the readings; it is not something you record at the bench. The units are what the headings are missing.
A heading without a unit does not say what the numbers are. Write 'Time / s' and 'Volume of gas / cm³'.
A title is never a mark. The unit in each heading is.

Use the same mass of calcium carbonate each time, for example 2.0 g.
Use the same volume and the same concentration of hydrochloric acid each time.
Start the stopwatch as the acid and the carbonate meet.
Record the volume of gas in the syringe at fixed times, for example every 10 s.

parts.workedSolution: Weigh out 2.0 g of large calcium carbonate chips and put them in a conical flask. Add 40 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid, close the flask with a bung and delivery tube leading to a gas syringe, and start the stopwatch at once. Record the volume of gas in the syringe every 10 s until it stops changing. Repeat the whole run with 2.0 g of powdered calcium carbonate and the same volume and concentration of acid. findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'The table shows the volume of carbon dioxide collected every 10 s. Use it to find the total volume of gas and the mean rate of reaction in cm³/s. [3]'
Her working:
studentWorking: The readings stop changing at 50 s, so the reaction took 50 s.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The gas syringe is never emptied, so each reading already contains all the gas collected so far. Adding the column counts the same gas seven times over. The total is the last reading, 54 cm³, which is the height of the flat stretch on the graph.
findTheMistake.feedback: The finishing time is right and the rule is right, so two of the three marks stand. Only the total goes: a syringe reading is a running total, so the answer is the last one, 54 cm³, and the rate becomes 1.08 cm³/s. Summer 2025's Booklet B report records this exact addition.

findTheMistake.stem:
Orla is asked: 'A gas syringe holds 29 cm³ of carbon dioxide at 15 s and 86 cm³ at 75 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction between 15 s and 75 s. [3]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Her time is right, but 86 cm³ is the reading at 75 s, not the change: the syringe already held 29 cm³ at 15 s. The change is 86 − 29 = 57 cm³.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the three marks: the time taken stands. The change is the later reading minus the earlier one, 57 cm³, so the rate is 0.95 cm³/s. The 2024 report records the same slip on a rate read off a graph: the readings right, the subtraction missed.

findings.asked: Plot gas volume against time for marble chips in acid, read the total volume and the finishing time, sketch the curve for powder, and draw the apparatus.
findings.wentWrong: The missing x-axis label was the commonest single loss. A sizeable number added every volume in the table instead of reading the plateau. Apparatus drawings were mostly good but must be flat, in section, with no line across a tube or stopper.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Labelled both axes with their units, plotted every point, drew one smooth curve, read the total off the flat stretch, and drew an open path from the flask to the syringe.
findings.rule: The total is the height of the plateau; the reaction ends where the curve goes flat.

findings.asked: Name the two labelled pieces of apparatus, the gas syringe and the conical flask, and give an observation during the reaction.
findings.wentWrong: Many left 'gas' out of 'gas syringe' or misspelled 'conical flask'; observations such as the gas box moving were too vague.
findings.rule: Name apparatus in full and spell it so it can be recognised: gas syringe, conical flask.

findings.asked: Find the decrease in mass from a mass-against-time graph, calculate the average rate and state its units, then sketch the curve for powder in place of lumps.
findings.wentWrong: Many gave incorrect units and scored 2 of 3 on the calculation. Sketches lost marks for running above the original curve, for two lines, and for not ending at the original finishing mass.
findings.rule: A rate's unit is the change's unit over seconds (g/s). On a falling mass graph a faster run lies below the original and ends at the same mass.

findings.asked: Calculate the rate of the fastest reaction to three decimal places, then sketch the curve for half the concentration.
findings.wentWrong: The arithmetic was usually right; the three-decimal-place instruction was what lost the mark, and some worked out all four rates when one was asked for. The half-concentration sketch scored 2 of 3 because it did not level off at 4 g, half the original 8 g: the thiosulfate was in excess, so the acid ran out first.
findings.rule: The reactant that runs out sets the final value: the same amounts give the same height, half of that reactant gives half the height, and a lower concentration is also a shallower curve.

findings.asked: Identify the apparatus used to measure a rate, then describe how the rate was measured.
findings.wentWrong: Few named the apparatus, and 'amount' written in place of mass or grams lost the marks for the method.
findings.rule: Say what you measure (mass in grams, volume in cm³) and over what time.

insight.ruleToRemember: Rate = change ÷ time, with the unit the change came in; rate = 1 ÷ time for one fixed change, in s⁻¹. On a graph the steepness is the rate, the flat part is the finish, and the height of the flat part is the total, set by the reactant that runs out. Read totals from the plateau, put units in every heading and axis label, and draw apparatus flat and open.
insight.aStarSignal: Sketching a changed run with the right steepness AND the right finishing height, and naming the reactant that runs out as the reason for that height.
